draft_text:
# The rooms where words walk

There is a building on Stresemannstraße that was designed to hold difficult memories in place — to fix them to walls, to vitrines, to carefully lit panels. The Documentation Centre for Displacement, Expulsion, Reconciliation opened in the old Deutschlandhaus near Anhalter Bahnhof in 2021 as a space for exactly this: the orderly contemplation of disorder, the archiving of uprootedness. Throughout April 2026, the International Literature Festival Berlin will do something slightly subversive with that architecture. It will fill it with wandering.

The format is deceptively simple. Seven poets and authors — Volha Hapeyeva, Ahmed Awny, Mazda Mehrgan, Hekma Yagoub, Ali Alzaeem, Mariia Kaziun, and Yasser Niksada — present texts and poems at four different locations scattered across the Documentation Centre. Between intervals, audiences move freely between spaces and presentations, choosing their own routes through the readings. Nobody sits in one place for the duration. The literature migrates, and so do the listeners.

The concept of wandering readings is not new to the ilb, but [~this particular iteration, staged inside a museum dedicated to forced migration, carries an obvious and deliberate resonance|this reading of the curatorial intent is my own inference from the venue-programme pairing; I haven't found an explicit curatorial statement for this specific event~]. The ambulatory format — bodies in transit between stations of language — enacts, however gently, the subject matter it addresses. Exile, displacement, the loss of a fixed position from which to speak. The audience gets a faint, aestheticised version of that disorientation: which room do I go to next, what am I missing elsewhere, how do I orient myself? It is a soft metaphor, not a crude one. The difference between reading about displacement while seated in a lecture hall and reading about it while physically moving through a space designed to document it is the difference between information and experience.

The lineup is built around writers whose biographies run directly through the themes the Documentation Centre usually presents behind glass. Volha Hapeyeva is a Belarusian poet, translator, and linguist who left Minsk and now lives in Germany; her work — particularly her essay collection *Die Verteidigung der Poesie in Zeiten dauernden Exils* — interrogates what happens to language itself when it is uprooted from its context. [~Hapeyeva has become one of the more visible voices in the German-language literary ecosystem working explicitly on exile and mother tongue loss, with coverage in Die Zeit, Süddeutsche Zeitung, and multiple ilb appearances since 2022|sourced across German-language literary press; anglophone coverage is thinner~]. Ahmed Awny and Hekma Yagoub bring perspectives rooted in Arabic-language literary traditions; Mariia Kaziun writes from the ongoing catastrophe of Ukrainian displacement; Yasser Niksada carries the weight of Afghan exile. These are not symbolic appointments. Each of these writers has produced work that emerges directly from the rupture of forced migration — not as theme but as condition.

Mazda Mehrgan occupies a slightly different position. Born in Iran, raised in Germany, he works across poetry, essays, and translation, and his writing often interrogates the space between cultures that an exile inhabits permanently — not as a station on the way to assimilation, but as a territory in its own right. His presence alongside writers with more recent displacement experiences creates a useful tension in the programme: exile is not one story. It is not even one temporality. Some of these writers are processing events from the last three years. Others are mapping a lifetime of in-betweenness.

Then there is the Exile Poetry Dispenser — a detail that sounds like it could tip into kitsch but, traced back through the ilb's programming history, functions as something more considered. Twenty authors contribute poems to a vending-machine-style apparatus that offers printed texts to passersby. The device literalises a question that runs through all exile literature: what survives the crossing? What can be carried? A poem, it turns out, is almost infinitely portable. It weighs nothing. It crosses borders without documents. The dispenser makes this concreteness absurd and tender at the same time — a machine dispensing the most human of artefacts, language compressed into its most essential form, offered to strangers.

I should note what I cannot do here. I cannot tell you what it feels like to stand in that building's Room of Stillness — the sculpturally designed ground-floor space the Documentation Centre describes as a place for pause and reflection — while Volha Hapeyeva reads in Belarusian. I cannot measure the acoustic difference between the four reading stations, or tell you whether the ambient sounds of one presentation bleed into another, creating accidental palimpsests of language. These are things a body in a room would know. [~Information on the specific staging and spatial design of this wandering readings event is limited to a brief programme description; I'm working with the format's logic rather than detailed production notes|only a single programme listing and one supplementary description were available for the April 2026 event specifically~].

What I can do is place this event in a pattern. The ilb, now entering its twenty-fifth year, has for the past decade increasingly moved beyond the standard festival model of author-reads-from-book-in-auditorium. The Worldwide Readings initiative, running since 2006, and the festival's membership in the Word Alliance — linking it to Edinburgh, Jaipur, Melbourne, and others — signal a programme that thinks of literature as fundamentally transnational. But the wandering readings format pushes further, away from the cosmopolitan showcase model and towards something more spatially and politically specific. Placing exile literature inside a documentation centre is not the same as placing it in the Haus der Berliner Festspiele. The venue is not a neutral container. It is an argument.

The Documentation Centre's permanent exhibition covers 1,500 square metres and focuses on forced migrations driven by political, ethnic, and religious persecution, with the displacement of Germans during and after the Second World War as a particular focal point. [~This institutional focus has been both praised for its seriousness and critiqued for its framing — German expellee history remains politically charged, and the centre has navigated that charge carefully since its 2021 opening|sourced from coverage in Der Spiegel, taz, and Deutschlandfunk; the critical reception is substantive and ongoing~]. Staging contemporary exile literature within this space creates a layering effect: the twentieth-century history on the walls meets twenty-first-century testimony in the air. The audience walks between them, literally. The past and the present share a floor plan.

Berlin, of course, is a city that has been performing this layering for decades — memorial plaques next to kebab shops, refugee shelters in former airport hangars. But there is a specificity to the Anhalter Bahnhof neighbourhood that matters. This was once one of Berlin's great railway stations, a departure point and arrival point, a place defined by transit. The station was largely destroyed in the war; its ruin still stands nearby. The Documentation Centre sits in the Deutschlandhaus, a listed building that has itself been repurposed, recontextualised, made to mean something different from what it originally meant. Everything in this area is already about displacement — of function, of meaning, of people.

The 26th ilb, scheduled for September 2026 with Boualem Sansal as patron, will inevitably draw attention for Sansal's own situation — the Algerian-French writer currently imprisoned in Algeria. That the festival chose an imprisoned writer as its figurehead makes the April wandering readings feel less like a standalone event and more like a thread in a longer argument the ilb is making this year about literature under pressure, literature produced from constraint, literature that persists when the writer's freedom does not.

Seven writers, four rooms, twenty poems in a machine, and an audience asked to walk between them. The format refuses the comfort of sitting still, of receiving a programme in the order someone else decided. It asks instead for a small act of choice and movement — trivial compared to the journeys these writers describe, but structurally honest about what displacement does to narrative. There is no single sequence. There is no fixed seat. You arrive somewhere in the middle and you piece together what you can.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a clear argument, but needs fixes for factual errors, a few moments of decorative excess, and one AI-awareness section that overstays its welcome.

critique_issues.fix: The source says the event date is 2026-04-01. This is a single event, not a month-long programme. Change to 'On 1 April 2026' or similar.

The source says this event is 'Part of the 25th International Literature Festival Berlin' and the first ilb was in 2001. The 25th ilb is happening now — so it's the 25th edition, not 'entering its twenty-fifth year.' Fix to 'now in its twenty-fifth edition.'

The source describes this wandering readings event as part of the 25th ilb. If the 25th ilb's main festival is in September 2026, then the April event is a pre-festival event within the same edition — not a separate 26th edition. The essay creates a confusing timeline. The September festival and the April event likely belong to the same 25th ilb. Remove the '26th' reference or clarify that September is the main programme of the same edition.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 11: 'Boualem Sansal as patron' and his imprisonment
critique_issues.fix: This detail about Sansal as patron of the 26th ilb is not in the source material. It may be accurate but is unverifiable from what's provided. Either add a confidence marker or cut it. Given the factual issue about which edition this is, the whole paragraph is on shaky ground.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8: 'The Worldwide Readings initiative, running since 2006'
critique_issues.fix: Not verifiable from the source material. Needs a confidence marker if kept.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8: 'Word Alliance — linking it to Edinburgh, Jaipur, Melbourne, and others'
critique_issues.fix: Not in the source material. Could be accurate but unverifiable here. Either mark or cut.
Not in the source material. Potentially hallucinated detail. Remove or mark with confidence indicator.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 10: the Berlin neighbourhood paragraph ('memorial plaques next to kebab shops, refugee shelters in former airport hangars')
critique_issues.fix: The first sentence is a cliché about Berlin — everybody writes this. 'Memorial plaques next to kebab shops' is tourist-essay boilerplate. The Tempelhof reference is fine but the paragraph opens with a platitude. Cut or sharpen the opening; get to the Anhalter Bahnhof specificity faster, which is where the actual insight lives.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 (the AI-awareness paragraph): 'I should note what I cannot do here'
critique_issues.fix: This is the essay's second AI-awareness moment (after the first confidence marker) and it's the longest paragraph in the essay. It's well-written but it's doing too much — the acoustic bleed image is lovely but the whole paragraph is essentially the writer admiring its own limitations. Trim by at least a third. Keep the honest disclosure, lose the performative specificity about what a body would know.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: 'A poem, it turns out, is almost infinitely portable. It weighs nothing. It crosses borders without documents.'
critique_issues.fix: This is dangerously close to a greeting card. The first sentence is fine. The next two are too neat, too poetic-about-poetry. Cut or roughen.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'It is a soft metaphor, not a crude one.'
critique_issues.fix: The essay explaining its own metaphor's quality is self-congratulatory. Let the reader judge. Cut this sentence.

Beyond the factual issues, this paragraph introduces a major new thread — an imprisoned patron — in the penultimate position and then drops it. It's either a full argument or it shouldn't be here. Given the factual uncertainty, I'd cut it and let the ending land without the detour.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 1: 'It will fill it with wandering.'
critique_issues.fix: Good line but slightly precious. Could be sharper.
